meanings.note: Informal encouragement to go or do something together; a shortened form of embora. Common in conversational Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we go to the meeting?

meanings.note: Informal reduced para. Before a feminine noun, this Brazilian spelling can also represent a contraction including the article a; the exact meeting is clear from context.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: A gathering of people for a purpose. Here a workplace meeting; the final diphthong is nasal.

examples.trans: I’m not going to the meeting.

meanings.note: A negative answer or a negation in a sentence. A final repeated não can reinforce a conversational refusal in Brazil.
Vou + infinitive can express a future intention: vou estar means I am going to be. Você takes the third-person vai.
Used here for being present at an event. Vou estar keeps estar in the infinitive after the finite form vou.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: One written contraction of em + essa. Feminine singular because reunião is feminine; at is natural English for attendance at a meeting.

examples.trans: I’m not going to be at that meeting.
Are you going to be at that meeting?

meanings.note: Introduces a contrast. The informal thanks softens the refusal; it does not accept the invitation.

examples.trans: It’s a meeting, but I’m not going.

meanings.note: The completed-past form valeu is also a conventional informal thanks in Brazil. In this scene it thanks the colleague for the invitation.

A person being addressed, with third-person verb agreement: você vai, vocês vão. Vai and vão are forms of ir, not forms of the pronoun. Common in Brazil; not a rule that every Brazilian region uses the same address system.

examples.trans: Are you going to the meeting?

meanings.note: Used for identifying a type of meeting or the department a person belongs to. The present forms sou and é are irregular.
Links a meeting with its subject. Do is de + the masculine article o; sou do financeiro identifies membership in the finance department.
An English loan used for the business activity of marketing. This line shortens the original marketing-planning meeting to a marketing meeting.
Subject form referring to the speaker. Explicit eu introduces his department in the explanation.
In this office, the masculine form stands for the finance department. The related adjective changes for gender and number; the department use is masculine singular.
Very common Brazilian exclamation expressing surprise, confusion, or pushback.
Means to ask a question (never to ask for a favour, which is pedir).

examples.text: Eu perguntei qual é o seu cargo?
examples.trans: Did I ask what your job title is?

meanings.note: Asks someone to identify one item or role, as in qual é o seu cargo.
Definite article agreeing in gender and number with its noun; also common before given names in casual Brazilian speech.

examples.trans: Look at the young woman over there.

meanings.note: Possessive determiner agreeing with the possessed noun; in Brazil it most often means your (with você).

examples.text: É isso que você quer pra sua vida?
examples.trans: Is that what you want for your life?

meanings.note: Official post or role inside a company.

examples.text: Ela mudou de cargo este ano.

meanings.note: All-purpose connector, relative link, question opener, and comparative word after mais or melhor.

examples.text: Eu acho que ele já foi.
examples.trans: I think that he already left.

meanings.note: Neutral demonstrative pronoun pointing to what was just said or done.
Informal masculine noun meaning guy, dude, or man; as a feminine noun it literally means face.
Used standalone or as calma aí! to tell someone to slow down and relax.
With que it is Brazil's most natural everyday way to say I think / do you think.

examples.text: Eu acho que você tá exagerando.

meanings.note: Comparative and superlative of bom; same singular form for masculine and feminine.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?

meanings.note: Alone as vocative gente! it means folks/guys; with article a gente it means we/us with third-person singular verbs.

examples.text: Você acha que é melhor que a gente?
examples.trans: Do you think you're better than us?
Oh, folks, the meeting ran late.

meanings.note: Refers to someone's time or duration (esse tempo inteiro).

examples.text: Seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?
I stayed there that whole time.

meanings.note: Marks comparisons (mais que), negated continuation (não ... mais, not anymore), and the farewell até mais.
First-person singular possessive agreeing with the thing possessed.

examples.text: O seu tempo vale mais que o meu?
examples.trans: Is your time worth more than mine?

meanings.note: Expresses possession, obligation in ter que + infinitive, and impersonal existence (tem alguns números, there are some numbers).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.

meanings.note: Takes present subjunctive entre after querer que (eu quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu tenho que entrar lá dentro.
examples.trans: I have to go inside there.
I want you to go in too.

meanings.note: Points to a place away from the speaker; lá dentro reinforces inside there.
Indicates the interior of a room or space, often paired with lá or para.
Expresses duration (por uma hora) and fixed phrases like por exemplo.

examples.trans: I stayed there for an hour.

meanings.note: Indefinite article; plural uns and umas mean some or a few in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.

examples.trans: Shall we have a little coffee?

meanings.note: Unit of sixty minutes or clock time.

examples.text: Vou ficar lá por uma hora.
examples.trans: I'm going to stay there for an hour.

examples.text: Já está na hora da reunião.
examples.trans: It's already time for the meeting.

meanings.note: Adds immediacy after imperatives like calma aí, or means there near you.
Limits a statement (eu só quero) or forms só que (except that / the catch is).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

examples.text: Só que agora ela precisa de ajuda.

meanings.note: Followed by an infinitive for your own wish (quero saber) or que + subjunctive for someone else (quero que você entre).

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: Covers knowing facts or finding out information.

examples.text: Eu só quero saber o motivo.
examples.trans: I just want to know the reason.

meanings.note: The cause or justification behind an action.

examples.trans: I want to know the reason for this.
There is no reason to shout.

meanings.note: Neutral contraction of de + isso, referring to a whole situation rather than a gendered noun.

examples.trans: I want to know the reason for this.

meanings.note: In até logo it looks ahead to the next meeting. The phrase is added as the lesson farewell, not quoted from the selected source window.
In the farewell até logo it anticipates meeting again. This is the time adverb, not a short form for a company logo.

examples.trans: I’ll go to the meeting soon.
